name: Abaz Arslanagić
milestone_by_age_26: Won World Championship bronze with Yugoslavia in 1970 and was named best goalkeeper of the tournament at age 25.
early_history_summary: Arslanagić began his handball career at RK Partizan Derventa at age 14 in 1958. He became a first-league goalkeeper with Partizan Belgrade before turning 18 in 1962, then moved to Borac Banja Luka in 1963 where he spent his entire prime. He debuted for the Yugoslav national team in 1969 and won World Championship bronze in 1970.
family_context_summary: Born in Derventa, Bosnia and Herzegovina; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Arslanagić started playing handball at 14 in his hometown of Derventa and became a first-league goalkeeper before 18, an unusually early debut. He joined Borac Banja Luka, one of Yugoslavia's top clubs, at 19 and developed into the national team goalkeeper by 25. Yugoslavia was a handball superpower in this era, providing an elite competitive ecosystem. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in Derventa, Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1944; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Retired from coaching in 2013; lives in Bosnia and Herzegovina at age 81.

name: Zlatko Portner

early_history_summary: Portner began his career with Sloga Hrtkovci and then Crvenka from 1980 to 1982. He joined Metaloplastika in 1982, becoming part of the legendary squad that won consecutive European Cup titles in 1984-85 and 1985-86 and six consecutive national championships. He won World Championship gold in his 1986 debut appearance for Yugoslavia.
family_context_summary: Born in Ruma, Serbia (then FPR Yugoslavia); family background not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Portner joined Metaloplastika at 20, one of Europe's premier handball clubs, and was surrounded by elite teammates including Veselin Vujović. The Yugoslav handball system was a global powerhouse in the 1980s, providing elite competition and coaching. He won back-to-back European Cups and World Championship gold by 24. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.

current_position: Died on September 23, 2020 in Switzerland at age 58; had retired from professional handball in 2002 after playing for Swiss clubs.

name: Iolanda Balaș
milestone_by_age_26: Set her first world record in the high jump in 1955 at age 18 (1.75m), and went on to win European Championships gold in 1958 and Olympic gold in 1960, all before age 26.
early_history_summary: Balaș was discovered at age 9 by her building's caretaker Luiza Ernst-Lupşa, a former national pentathlon champion, in Timișoara. She won her first national title at 14 in 1951, took European Championships silver at 17 in 1954, and set her first world record at 18 in 1955. She moved to Bucharest in 1953 to train under coach Ion Söter, whom she later married.
family_context_summary: Born to a Romanian-Hungarian family in Timișoara; mother Etel Bozó was a housewife, father Frigyes was a locksmith of Hungarian descent who was separated from the family after WWII. The family experienced wartime hardship and poverty.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family domain advantage; Balaș was discovered by a neighbor, former athlete Luiza Ernst-Lupşa, who spotted her talent at age 9.
evidence_summary: Balaș was discovered at age 9 by her apartment building's caretaker, Luiza Ernst-Lupşa, a former national pentathlon champion, who spotted her natural jumping talent. She was then coached by Ion Söter, a former national high jump champion, from a young age. Despite growing up in poverty with an absent father after WWII, she won her first national title at 14 and set her first world record at 18. Her height of 1.85m and natural athletic ability were significant physical advantages.
starting_point: Born in Timișoara, Romania in 1936 to a working-class Romanian-Hungarian family; father was a locksmith who was separated from the family after WWII, and the family lived in poverty.
current_position: Died on March 11, 2016 in Bucharest at age 79; served as President of the Romanian Athletics Federation from 1988 to 2005.

trajectory.event: Won her first of 19 national high jump titles.

Died on March 11, 2016 in Bucharest, Romania.

name: Juan Carlos Ferrero
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first ATP Tour title at the Majorca Open in 1999 at age 19 and was named ATP Newcomer of the Year; later won the French Open and reached world No. 1 in 2003 at age 23.
early_history_summary: Ferrero began playing tennis at age 7 with his father Eduardo. At age 9, he was taken to coach Antonio Martínez Cascales' academy in Villena, Alicante, who remained his lifelong coach. He reached the Junior French Open final in 1998 at age 18, then won his first ATP title in 1999 at 19. His mother Rosario died of cancer when he was 16, which deepened his resolve to dedicate himself to tennis.
family_context_summary: Born in Ontinyent, Spain; father Eduardo Ferrero Micó was a tennis player who taught him the sport from age 7. Mother Rosario died of cancer when Ferrero was 16. He has two older sisters.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Eduardo played tennis and introduced Ferrero to the sport at age 7, providing early domain exposure and equipment access.
evidence_summary: Ferrero's father introduced him to tennis at 7 and at 9 he was placed under the guidance of Antonio Martínez Cascales, who coached him for his entire career. The Cascales academy in Villena provided elite training facilities and peer group. Spain was a clay-court tennis powerhouse, providing a strong competitive ecosystem. His mother's death when he was 16 intensified his dedication. He reached the Junior French Open final at 18 and won his first ATP title at 19.
starting_point: Born in Ontinyent, Spain in 1980; father Eduardo was a tennis player who introduced him to the sport, mother Rosario was a homemaker who died of cancer when he was 16.
current_position: Runs the JC Ferrero-Equelite Tennis Academy in Villena, Alicante; former coach of Carlos Alcaraz (2019-2024); estimated net worth in the millions from prize money (~$14M career) and academy revenue.

name: Mihaela Stănuleț
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal in the team all-around at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics at age 17, plus European Championships bronze on beam and World Championships team silver in 1983 at age 16.
early_history_summary: Stănuleț started gymnastics at age 8 at CSȘ Sibiu under coach Nicolae Buzoianu. She trained at the Romanian national team center in Deva from 1980 to 1985. She competed internationally from 1979, won the Balkan All-Around Championship in 1982 at 15, and earned European and World medals in 1983 before winning Olympic team gold in 1984.
family_context_summary: Born in Sibiu, Romania; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Stănuleț entered the Romanian gymnastics pipeline at age 8, training at CSȘ Sibiu before moving to the national team center in Deva at 13. Romania was a world-dominant gymnastics power in this era, providing elite coaching from Octavian Bellu, Adrian Goreac, and others. She won Balkan, European, World, and Olympic medals between ages 15 and 17. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in Sibiu, Romania in 1967; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Works as a gymnastics coach at CSȘ Sibiu, the same club where she trained as a child; received Honorary Citizen of Sibiu in 2020.

name: Mordechai Vanunu
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26. Vanunu completed military service (1971-74) and began working as a technician at the Dimona nuclear plant in 1976 at age 24. His famous act of revealing Israel's nuclear secrets occurred in 1986 at age 34.
early_history_summary: Vanunu was born in Marrakesh, Morocco and emigrated to Israel with his family at age 10. He completed military service as a First Sergeant in a sappers unit from 1971 to 1974, then began working at the Dimona nuclear plant in 1976. He started studying philosophy and geography at Ben Gurion University in 1979 and graduated in 1984-85. He was laid off from Dimona in November 1985 and revealed nuclear secrets to the Sunday Times in 1986.
family_context_summary: Born in Marrakesh, Morocco to an Orthodox Jewish family of 11 children; father ran a grocery store, mother was a housewife. Family emigrated to Israel in 1963 and settled in impoverished Beersheba, initially living in a hut without electricity.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family domain advantage; father was a grocery store owner in Morocco who emigrated to Israel.
evidence_summary: Vanunu's notability comes entirely from his 1986 whistleblowing act at age 34, when he revealed details of Israel's nuclear weapons program to the Sunday Times. By age 26, he had completed military service and was beginning work as a technician at Dimona — no material public milestone had occurred. His fame arrived more than a decade later.

Drafted 6th overall by the Edmonton Oilers in 1980, he led all NHL defensemen in scoring in just his second season.
family_context_summary: Born in Weston, Ontario and grew up in Malton, a working-class community near Toronto. Father delivered bread for a living and adjusted his work schedule to attend Coffey's games. Family was supportive but not wealthy.
